title: Implications of labour turnover

blocks.heading: Definition
blocks.text: Labour turnover is the rate at which employees leave a business during a stated period. The percentage alone does not show who left, why they left or whether replacements were recruited.

blocks.heading: Worked application
blocks.text: A private hospital losing experienced nurses may face greater disruption than a clothing retailer losing temporary holiday staff. Nurses require specialist qualifications, understand clinical procedures and maintain patient relationships, so replacement takes longer and the consequences for service quality may be more serious.

blocks.heading: Analysis
blocks.text: High labour turnover can create repeated recruitment, induction and training costs. Replacement employees may initially work more slowly or require additional supervision, so average costs may rise and service capacity may fall.

blocks.heading: Low labour turnover
blocks.text: Low labour turnover can reduce replacement costs and help retain experience, customer knowledge and stable working relationships. However, extremely low turnover may also limit promotion opportunities and the arrival of new ideas.

blocks.heading: Judgement
blocks.text: No single labour-turnover rate is automatically good or bad. Managers should identify which employees are leaving, the reason for departure, replacement difficulty and the organisation objective before deciding whether intervention is required.
